When America Married Youngest

# When America Married Youngest

Women’s age at first marriage hit its lowest point in the 1950s, then climbed about eight years — alongside a steady rise in women’s share of college degrees.

By Karina Advani

## The picture in your head is probably wrong

Ask almost anyone how people used to marry and you’ll hear the same thing: young. Teenage brides, early-twenties grooms, a wedding barely out of school — that was simply how it was done “back then.” It’s a tidy picture, and for one stretch of the twentieth century it holds up. But line up more than a hundred years of Census records, and the picture changes.

In 1890, the typical American woman married for the first time at 22.0. By 1956 she was marrying at 20.1 — the youngest age anywhere in the table. Then the numbers turned around and kept climbing, all the way to 28.4 in 2025. The “traditional” wedding age many of us imagine turns out to be a dip, not a baseline.

## First, what does “median age at first marriage” mean?

Imagine lining up every woman who married for the first time in a given year, youngest to oldest. The median is the person standing in the middle: half married younger than that age, half married older. Unlike an average, a few very early or very late weddings can’t drag it around.

Two details matter. “First marriage” leaves out remarriages. And the Census Bureau estimates the figure from surveys rather than counting every wedding. The table we use here gives separate medians for women and for men, so we can watch both.

## The story in three parts

### Part 1 · 1890 to the 1950s: a long slide downward

In 1890, the median woman married at 22.0 and the median man at 26.1. For the next several decades the ages drifted down. By 1940 they were 21.5 for women and 24.3 for men, and by 1956 they hit the floor: 20.1 for women and 22.5 for men. That’s the lowest point anywhere in the table, which runs from 1890 to 2025.

Women’s age fell by nearly two years between 1890 and 1956 (22.0 down to 20.1); men’s fell by 3.6 years (26.1 down to 22.5). The 1950s weren’t the norm that earlier generations handed down. They were the bottom of a slope.

20.1 years The median age at which American women first married in 1956 — the youngest in the whole table.

### Part 2 · The climb since the 1950s

Then the slide reversed. Women’s median age was 20.3 in 1960; by 1980 it had reached 22.0 — exactly where it stood in 1890. It didn’t stop there. It kept rising through the decades that followed, to 28.4 in 2025. That’s about 8.3 years above the 1956 low (or 8.1 above 1960) — roughly eight years.

One note on the record itself: until 1940 the Census counted marriage ages only once a decade. Yearly estimates begin in 1947, so there is a gap in the data for 1941–46. We leave that gap empty rather than guess.

22.0 in 1890. 22.0 in 1980. It took until 1980 for women’s median age at first marriage to climb back to where it started in 1890.

### Part 3 · Where things stand in 2025

In the most recent year in the table, the median woman married for the first time at 28.4 and the median man at 30.8 — a gap of 2.4 years. Women’s estimate was 28.6 in 2024 (and in 2021, after revision), so 2025 is a touch lower. The Census Bureau flags that its 2025 estimates use new population figures, so treat a one-year wiggle with caution; the decades-long direction is what matters.

## Now add college

The second table, from the National Center for Education Statistics, counts the bachelor’s degrees colleges award each year and splits them by sex. It lets us ask what share of those degrees went to women.

The long view is a story of steady gains with one sharp interruption. Women earned 14.7% of bachelor’s degrees in 1869–70 and 17.3% in 1889–90. By 1939–40 that had grown to 41.3% (76,954 women out of 186,500 graduates).

Then came the dip. In 1949–50, women earned just 23.9% — the lowest share since 1909–10, when it was 22.7%. The tables show what happened: the total number of degrees more than doubled in a decade, from 186,500 to 432,058, but men’s degrees tripled (109,546 to 328,841) while women’s grew far less (76,954 to 103,217). Historians often link that surge in male graduates to veterans returning from World War II — an explanation that comes from outside these two tables, so take it as context rather than something this data proves.

After that, women’s share climbed again: 35.3% by 1959–60, 43.1% in 1969–70, and past the halfway mark for the first time in 1981–82 (49.8% the year before, 50.3% that year). The most recent actual year, 2021–22, stands at 58.5% (1,179,719 women out of 2,015,035 graduates).

23.9% → 58.5% Women’s share of bachelor’s degrees, from the 1949–50 dip to 2021–22, the latest year of actual data.

Put the two stories side by side and they share a shape. Marriage ages and women’s share of degrees both bottomed out around the middle of the twentieth century, and both have climbed over the same decades since. The figure below shows them on one timeline.

Women’s median age at first marriage rose from 20.3 in 1960 to 28.4 in 2025, while their share of bachelor’s degrees rose from 35.3% in 1959–60 to 58.5% in 2021–22.

## What this data can’t tell us

- Rising together is not proof of a link. Marriage ages and women’s share of degrees moved in the same direction over the same decades, but these two tables can’t show that one drove the other. Other things were changing at the same time: access to birth control, the economy and the cost of living, jobs open to women, and shifting attitudes about when — and whether — to marry. This data can’t sort those out.
- The median says nothing about whether people marry at all. It describes the typical age among people who do marry; it doesn’t tell us how many people never do.
- Same-sex marriages are included starting in 2019. The Census Bureau notes that estimates from 2019 on count same-sex married couples, so recent numbers are not strictly comparable with earlier ones.
- The early record is thin. From 1890 to 1940 the Census measured marriage age only once every ten years, and there is nothing for 1941–46. Degree counts are also spaced ten years apart until 1979–80. Dotted lines in the figure mark those stretches; they are not a claim about the years in between.
- A single year can wobble. The Census Bureau notes that 2025 reflects new population estimates, which can nudge a single year’s number.
